extracted.intended_audience: journalism students and reporters learning news writing (court reporters)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and illustrative examples for writing news stories about criminal and civil court matters, showing both routine (fact-first) and human-interest (feature) approaches to court reporting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bring out human interest in routine news
rubrics_metrics.description: Note — The way in which the human interest can be brought out in what might ordinarily be considered routine news, is shown by the second of the following two stories.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use human-interest angles to make routine court or legal items more engaging for readers; compare a straightforward factual report with a humanized narrative (example: the Janin hydroaeroplane story is presented with personal detail, celebration scenes, and quotes to highlight human interest).

rubrics_metrics.name: Report legal outcomes and official orders clearly
rubrics_metrics.description: Include formal legal actions and outcomes such as verdicts, appointments (conservator), orders restoring rights, releases from institutions, suits filed, receivership appointments, and assignments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: State the decision or legal action early and precisely (examples: jury verdict finding Baptiste insane; Judge Owens' order restoring Baptiste; Probate Judge Gregg ordering restoration of funds; receivership proceedings for Robert Z. Link & Co.; assignment of Henry W. Williams for benefit of creditors).

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide background and personal history for parties
rubrics_metrics.description: Give the relevant life history or prior circumstances of the persons involved (marriage history, previous incidents, prior institutional actions) so readers understand context.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include chronological background that explains how the present action arose (examples: Mrs. Hansen's seventeen years of alleged abuse and marriage timeline; Dr. and Mrs. Smith's married life from 1900 to 1913; Leon Welfish's immigration and hospitalization history).

rubrics_metrics.name: Cite official sources and documentary evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Use and identify affidavits, depositions, court records, investigators' findings, hospital records, immigration officials' statements, and auditors as sources for claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mention the documentary basis for allegations or facts (examples: Mrs. Hansen accompanied by affidavits and a deposition from her son; investigators at the Italian consul's office; bankers' audit that revealed misleading statements).

rubrics_metrics.name: Include concrete financial and material details
rubrics_metrics.description: Report specific monetary amounts, costs, inventories, and other measurable details when relevant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: List sums and material particulars to ground stories in facts (examples: Baptiste had about $96; funeral expenses of $8 hearse, $35 headstone, $11 coaches; company debts and bankholdings of nearly $2,500,000; estimates of liabilities and stock issues).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use direct quotations and dialogue to convey voice
rubrics_metrics.description: Incorporate verbatim quotes from principals, officials, witnesses, or participants to show voice, attitude, and reaction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quotes humanize and authenticate reporting (examples: quoted phrases like "We make the buryings," Mr. Arthur's explanations about vegetarianism and trade, Janin's remarks about his invention and future plans).

rubrics_metrics.name: Present competing explanations and sides
rubrics_metrics.description: When controversies or explanations differ, report the rival accounts and the parties offering them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include both the critics' and principals' versions so readers can see the dispute (examples: company secretary William H. Arthur's explanation vs. bankers' audit findings about misleading statements; Curtiss's account of motor power vs. Janin's prior drawings and the patent examiners' findings).

rubrics_metrics.name: Narrate events in chronological sequence where helpful
rubrics_metrics.description: When telling a case story (e.g., an inquiry, trial, or personal saga), present the sequence of events clearly so readers can follow cause and effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use dates and sequential markers (examples: timeline of Baptiste's arrest, jury verdict on July 2, coming to July 4 and calling for trousers, release a month later; Janin's decade-long experiments leading to the 1910/1911 decision).

rubrics_metrics.name: Identify institutional actors and give titles
rubrics_metrics.description: Name judges, receivers, attorneys, boards, hospital authorities, company officers, and other institutional actors with their official titles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Attributing actions to properly identified officials clarifies authority and responsibility (examples: County Judge John E. Owens, Probate Judge Gregg, Receiver William T. Harrison, Secretary William H. Arthur, Board of Examiners of the Patent Office).

rubrics_metrics.name: Explain legal and financial mechanisms when relevant
rubrics_metrics.description: Describe procedures like receivership, conservatorship, assignment for benefit of creditors, court orders, and patent-examination processes to make the legal/financial significance clear.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Give enough procedural detail for readers to understand consequences (examples: conservator appointed for funds and statutory one-year limitation; banks placing an auditing firm on the books discovering discrepancies; how a patent Board of Examiners resolves interference claims).

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose an appropriate tone/lead — routine fact-first or human-feature
rubrics_metrics.description: Decide whether the story is presented as a straightforward routine report emphasizing outcomes and facts, or as a human-feature that foregrounds people and emotions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the routine lead for straightforward legal notices and the human-feature approach when there is an opportunity to dramatize personal stakes (the page pairs two versions of the hydroaeroplane/patent story: a factual account and a human-interest narrative showing speech, celebration, and personal detail).
